L	There was a time, and it was many years ago now, when I had to stay in a hospital for almost nine
weeks. This was in New York City, and at night a view of the Chrysler Building, with its
geometric brilliance of lights, was directly visible from my bed. During the day, the building’s
beauty receded, and gradually it became simply one more large structure against a blue sky, and
all the city’s buildings seemed remote, silent, far away. It was May, and then June, and I
remember how I would stand and look out the window at the sidewalk below and watch the young
women— my age— in their spring clothes, out on their lunch breaks; I could see their heads
moving in conversation, their blouses rippling in the breeze. I thought how when I got out of the
hospital I would never again walk down the sidewalk without giving thanks for being one of those
people, and for many years I did that— I would remember the view from the hospital window and
be glad for the sidewalk I was walking on.
To begin with, it was a simple story: I had gone into the hospital to have my appendix out. After
two days they gave me food, but I couldn’t keep it down. And then a fever arrived. No one could
isolate any bacteria or figure out what had gone wrong. No one ever did. I took fluids through one
IV, and antibiotics came through another. They were attached to a metal pole on wobbly wheels
that I pushed around with me, but I got tired easily. Toward the beginning of July, whatever
problem had taken hold of me went away. But until then I was in a very strange state— a literally
feverish waiting— and I really agonized. I had a husband and two small daughters at home; I
missed my girls terribly, and I worried about them so much I was afraid it was making me sicker.
Source: An extract from My Name is Lucy Barton by Elizabeth Strout

II.	Sitting on his father’s desk chair, Marvin swung his feet, which didn’t quite reach the floor. He
drew spirals in the margins of his school notes while he waited, and every once in a while he
checked the message on his tablet; for more than ten minutes now it had been displaying the
words Establishing connection. Below that was the warning This procedure could take some time.
It was information meant for those who had never started up a kentuki before. Marvin, on the
other hand, had already witnessed the exciting first connections that two of his friends had made.
He knew what steps to follow.
A week before, when his father had discovered Marvin’s real grades, he’d made him promise to sit
in the study for three hours every day, surrounded by books, doing homework. Marvin had said, “I
swear to God that I will sit for three hours a day at the desk surrounded by books,” but he hadn’t
said anything about studying, so he wasn’t really going back on his word. And it would be months
before his father caught on that he’d installed a kentuki on the tablet—that is, if his father ever
found the time to discover anything else about his son again. Marvin had paid for the kentuki
connection using his mother’s savings account. It was digital money, the only kind the dead can
have. Marvin had already used that account on other occasions, and he was starting to suspect
that not even his father knew it existed.
Source: An extract from Little Eyes by Samanta Schweblin, translated by Megan McDowell

III.	On an evening in the latter part of May a middle-aged man was walking homeward from Shaston
to the village of Marlott, in the adjoining Vale of Blakemore, or Blackmoor. The pair of legs that
carried him were rickety, and there was a bias in his gait which inclined him somewhat to the left
of a straight line. He occasionally gave a smart nod, as if in confirmation of some opinion, though
he was not thinking of anything in particular. An empty egg-basket was slung upon his arm, the
nap of his hat was ruffled, a patch being quite worn away at its brim where his thumb came in
taking it off. Presently he was met by an elderly parson astride on a gray mare, who, as he rode,
hummed a wandering tune. "Good night t'ee," said the man with the basket. "Good night, Sir
John," said the parson. The pedestrian, after another pace or two, halted, and turned round. "Now,
sir, begging your pardon; we met last market-day on this road about this time, and I said 'Good
night,’ and you made reply 'Good night, Sir John,' as now." "I did," said the parson. "And once
before that—near a month ago." "I may have." "Then what might your meaning be in calling me
‘Sir John' these different times, when I be plain Jack Durbeyfield, the haggler?" The parson rode a
step or two nearer. "It was only my whim," he said; and, after a moment's hesitation: "It was on
account of a discovery I made some little time ago, whilst I was hunting up pedigrees for the new
county history. I am Parson Tringham, the antiquary, of Stagfoot Lane. Don't you really know,
Durbeyfield, that you are the lineal representative of the ancient and knightly family of the
d'Urbervilles, who derive their descent from Sir Pagan d'Urberville, that renowned knight who
came from Normandy with William the Conqueror, as appears by Battle Abbey Roll?" "Never
heard it before, sir!" "Well it's true. Throw up your chin a moment, so that I may catch the profile
of your face better. Yes, that's the d'Urberville nose and chin—a little debased."

IV.	It was my father who made the arrangements. My uncle helped, since he lived down south, where
all this kind of business is carried out. I’m talking south-south: down past the airport, past the
swamp, past the oilfields, everything. Way down at the bottom of the island, down where
Columbus landed, long ago. There’s hardly anything down there, just fishing villages. Peaceful,
old-time places: a few ramshackle wooden houses, and children playing marbles in the shade
under the trees. Everywhere you look, in those places, you see pirogues pulled up onto the sand:
little wooden boats, fishing boats, supposedly — although how much fishing the men really do
nowadays is anybody’s guess. The boats are very basic. Open-topped, maybe twenty feet long, with
just a plank of wood to sit on and a boat-engine clamped onto the back. But somehow they manage
to make the journey across those seven miles of ocean between Trinidad and Venezuela — and
carrying all kinds of things, not just fish. It’s a dangerous journey, though, even when special
arrangements are made, as they were for me.
My father brought me the clothes I was to wear: black T-shirt and long-pants; a big long-sleeved
men’s shirt to wear over the T-shirt, also in black, and with the buttons cut out. We’d be travelling
by night, and anything that might catch in torchlight had to be covered, including my own skin.
The Trinidad and Tobago Coast Guard was one difficulty, the Guardia Nacional on the Venezuelan
side was another, but the worst problem was bandits. Bandits would steal the engine off the back
of the boat and leave you out there to drift, or they would take the whole boat, and throw you in

the sea. I also had a pillowcase to go over my head: the reflection of torchlight against things like
eyeballs and teeth had been known to give people away.
Source: An extract from Love Forms by Claire Adam

IV.	It was my father who made the arrangements. My uncle helped, since he lived down south, where
all this kind of business is carried out. I’m talking south-south: down past the airport, past the
swamp, past the oilfields, everything. Way down at the bottom of the island, down where
Columbus landed, long ago. There’s hardly anything down there, just fishing villages. Peaceful,
old-time places: a few ramshackle wooden houses, and children playing marbles in the shade
under the trees. Everywhere you look, in those places, you see pirogues pulled up onto the sand:
little wooden boats, fishing boats, supposedly — although how much fishing the men really do
nowadays is anybody’s guess. The boats are very basic. Open-topped, maybe twenty feet long, with
just a plank of wood to sit on and a boat-engine clamped onto the back. But somehow they manage
to make the journey across those seven miles of ocean between Trinidad and Venezuela — and
carrying all kinds of things, not just fish. It’s a dangerous journey, though, even when special
arrangements are made, as they were for me.
My father brought me the clothes I was to wear: black T-shirt and long-pants; a big long-sleeved
men’s shirt to wear over the T-shirt, also in black, and with the buttons cut out. We’d be travelling
by night, and anything that might catch in torchlight had to be covered, including my own skin.
The Trinidad and Tobago Coast Guard was one difficulty, the Guardia Nacional on the Venezuelan
side was another, but the worst problem was bandits. Bandits would steal the engine off the back
of the boat and leave you out there to drift, or they would take the whole boat, and throw you in

the sea. I also had a pillowcase to go over my head: the reflection of torchlight against things like
eyeballs and teeth had been known to give people away.
Source: An extract from Love Forms by Claire Adam

VI. “Vande Mataram,” composed by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay in the 1870s and published in
his novel Anandamath in 1882, has remained one of India’s most iconic patriotic songs. The
phrase means “I bow to thee, Mother,” symbolizing devotion and respect for the motherland. In
2026, India celebrates 150 years of Vande Mataram, marking a century and a half of its
inspiration in the freedom struggle and national consciousness.
During the Indian independence movement, “Vande Mataram” became more than a song—it was a
rallying cry. Freedom fighters and ordinary citizens sang it to inspire courage and unity against
British rule. The song, written in Sanskritized Bengali, beautifully blends devotion to the nation
with a call for selfless action and sacrifice.
Even today, it continues to evoke patriotism. Schools, public events, and national ceremonies
feature it as a reminder of India’s struggle for freedom and the spirit of unity. Celebrating 150
years of “Vande Mataram” honors not only Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay’s literary genius but
also the enduring love and respect Indians hold for their motherland.

during personal time. This continuous engagement disrupts work-life balance and negatively
affects mental health, family relationships, and overall well-being.

boundaries. Such measures promote healthier workplaces, improve productivity, and reduce

efficient during working hours.www.lawpreptutorial.com

employees. Organizations must establish clear guidelines regarding after-hours communication,

avoiding work, but about ensuring balance, dignity, and respect in professional life. In a fast-paced
digital world, safeguarding personal time is essential for sustainable growth and well-being.

XI.	The doctrine of vicarious liability lies at the heart of all common law systems of tort law. It
represents not a tort itself, but a rule of responsibility which renders the defendant liable for the
tortious act of another. In its most common form, it renders an employer liable for the torts
committed by an employee in the course of employment. Traditionally, fault is seen as the core
basis for liability in tort law; however, the common law has embraced vicarious liability as a form
of strict liability where the employer is held responsible regardless of their own personal fault. The
focus is on the fact that the employer, in the pursuit of profit, has placed confidence in employees
who have subsequently harmed others.
Courts have reformulated the scope of this liability to include injuries caused by a "tortious risk"—

questions.stimulus:
XI. ‘Quantum meruit' is a Latin phrase meaning 'what one has earned.' In the context of contract law,
it serves as a remedy where a person has rendered services or provided materials under
circumstances that imply a promise to pay, even if an enforceable express contract was never
finalized or was later breached. The whole concept behind this solution is that the work done
should be paid for, and the other party should not be unjustly enriched by the former party's act. It
is a solution available under Indian contract law to ensure fairness when a contract is mutually
modified or deemed unenforceable due to a technical deficiency.
Recovery in quantum meruit is appropriate where the parties, which are not at fault themselves,
by their conduct, have formed a relationship that is contractual in nature. For example, if a
written agreement between an owner and a contractor is deemed unenforceable because it violates
public policy or has a technical flaw, the contractor may still recover for the reasonable value of
the labor performed. Since specific terms in an implied contract are absent, the law supplies the
missing contract price by asking what one would have to pay in the open market for the same
work. Thus, the measure of damages is defined as the reasonable market value of the materials
furnished and the labor performed.
Source: Journal of Gujarat Research Society & Law Mantra ("Doctrine of Quantum Meruit under
Indian Contract Act")

questions.stimulus:
XIII. The doctrine of separation of powers is intended to remove the abuse of power by authorities by
ensuring that no single organ of the government exercises power beyond its constitutional
mandate. This doctrine is generally based on four pillars: the Exclusivity Principle, which divides
government into three structural organs; the Functional Principle, which prevents one organ from
performing the tasks of another; the Check and Balance Principle, which mandates that organs
oversee each other to ensure actions remain within legal bounds; and the Mutuality Principle,
which encourages cooperation rather than confrontation between branches. In India, while the
doctrine is not expressly mentioned in the Constitution with "pedantic rigor,” it is recognized as a
part of the Basic Structure.
In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, the Supreme Court ruled that the separation of
powers among the legislature, executive, and judiciary is a fundamental feature of the
Constitution that cannot be amended. This framework does not imply a rigid or absolute
separation, as there is some overlap; for instance, the President has certain legislative powers, and
the judiciary has the power of judicial review over executive and legislative acts. The goal of this
demarcation is to avoid the suppression of rights that occurs when power is concentrated in a
single group. By allowing each branch to specialize and providing instruments like the judicial
power to declare laws unconstitutional, the system maintains a sensible approximation of
autonomy while preventing arbitrariness.
Source: International Journal of Innovative Law Research ("Separation of Power") & JGU
Institutional Repository.

XIV. The doctrine of caveat emptor, or "let the buyer beware," is a cornerstone of commercial law based
on the principle that the buyer must exercise their own skill and judgment when purchasing a
product. It implies that in the absence of fraud, misrepresentation, or active concealment, the
seller is under no duty to disclose defects in the goods. If a buyer examines a product and is
satisfied with its condition, they generally have no subsequent right to return it or claim damages
if they later discover a defect. This rule places the onus on the consumer to be cautious and to
protect their own rights through reasonable examination before a transaction is finalized.
However, the doctrine is not absolute and is subject to significant exceptions. It does not apply
where the buyer expressly or impliedly informs the seller of the specific purpose for which the
goods are required, relying on the seller’s expertise, or where the goods are bought by description
from a seller who deals in such items. In modern times, judicial trends have seen a shift toward
caveat venditor ("let the seller beware"), particularly in consumer protection cases where there is a
significant information asymmetry between the parties. Nevertheless, caveat emptor remains the
default rule for public auctions and many private sales of specific goods, serving as a reminder
that the law expects a basic level of diligence from every purchaser.
Source: Indian Journal of Legal Review (IJLR 2024) & Vanderbilt Law Review.

Al-powered surveillance systems in public spaces. Proponents argue that these technologies,
equipped with facial recognition and behavioural analysis, significantly reduce crime rates by
enabling real-time threat detection. For instance, cities like London and Singapore report a 20-
30% drop in petty crimes since implementation. The reasoning is straightforward: deterrence
through omnipresence. When potential offenders know they are being watched by an unblinking
digital eye, rational choice theory suggests they will opt for compliance over transgression.
Moreover, these systems allow law enforcement to allocate resources efficiently, focusing human
officers on high-risk interventions rather than routine patrols.

panopticon society where citizens self-censor out of fear. Ethical concerns intensify with
documented cases of algorithmic bias—studies show facial recognition tools misidentify people of
colour at rates up to 35% higher than others, leading to wrongful detentions. This not only
undermines trust in institutions but also perpetuates systemic inequalities. Governments counter
that anonymization protocols and human oversight mitigate these risks, yet evidence from
independent audits reveals persistent flaws. The core tension lies in balancing collective security
against individual liberty: is the marginal crime reduction worth the slippery slope toward
totalitarianism? Policymakers must assume that technological perfection is unattainable; thus,
robust regulatory frameworks—such as mandatory transparency reports and independent
audits—are essential. Without them, public backlash could stall innovation. Ultimately, the
argument hinges on societal values: a polity prioritizing safety may embrace surveillance, while
one valuing autonomy might reject it. As AI evolves, the debate demands nuanced reasoning, not
binary absolutes, to forge policies that neither stifle progress nor sacrifice principles.

XVII. Tune in to the U-19 World Cup, and regional South Asian dialects would be almost as audible as
the English twang. There is a Hindi speaker in 10 of the 16 teams that participate in the
tournament; there is at least one cricketer who understands Punjabi in seven teams; and one who
can speak Gujarati, Telugu and Malayalam in four teams. There are Urdu, Tamil, Sinhala, and
Marathi speakers in teams from outside the Subcontinent. Among the 240 cricketers that have
descended on Namibia and Zimbabwe, 92 are either South Asians or have South Asian ancestors,
constituting 26 per cent of the tournament’s stable of players. The pattern is a reflection of the
shifting sands in world cricket. A game that was once segregated on racial lines in Africa, divided
along social lines in England and Australia, that once saw a prominent British politician, Lord
Tebbit, envisage a “loyalty test” for migrants, has become more inclusive and diverse. Two
youngsters of Pakistani descent are the pillars of the England team; two Indians and two Sri
Lankans are regulars in Australia’s side. New Zealand has four Indians. The USA team fielded an
entire side of second-generation Indians, even as their president, Donald Trump, is on a fierce
visa-revoking spree. Cricket is no longer a colonial sport, it has embraced the post-colonial spirit.
The next stage in the evolution would be akin to the situation in football, where immigrants form
the crux of most European powerhouses, notably England, France, Spain, Belgium and Portugal.
The previously rigid Italy, too, has opened the doors for migrants. Similarly, the identity of cricket
as a colonial leftover has changed, as British society has integrated migrants from its former
colonies. The story of migration is also reshaping the world of sports.
Source: From Under 19 World Cup, a message: Cricket has embraced migrant & post-colonial
spirit, Indian Express
